Afghanistan.history: Initially adopted in 2006, the anthem was written by Abdul Bari Jahani. Its lyrics mention various ethnic groups of Afghanistan and emphasize national unity.
Afghanistan.funFact: The lyrics are required by the constitution to be in Pashto and to mention 'Allah is the Greatest' (Allahu Akbar).

Argentina.history: Adopted in 1813, the lyrics were written by Vicente López y Planes and the music by Blas Parera. It was originally much longer and included strong anti-Spanish sentiment.
Argentina.funFact: The official version today actually only uses the introduction and the final parts of the original song, as the anti-Spanish verses were removed to maintain diplomatic relations.

Australia.history: Written by Peter Dodds McCormick in 1878, it originally had four verses. It officially replaced 'God Save the Queen' as the national anthem in 1984.
Australia.funFact: In 2021, a single word was changed: 'For we are young and free' became 'For we are one and free' to better reflect Indigenous history.

Brazil.history: Composed in 1831 by Francisco Manuel da Silva, it remained without official lyrics for nearly 90 years. The current patriotic lyrics were adopted in 1922.
Brazil.funFact: It is famous for its long, dramatic orchestral introduction before the singing actually begins.

Canada.history: Originally commissioned by Lieutenant Governor Théodore Robitaille for Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day in 1880. It became the official national anthem in 1980.
Canada.funFact: The lyrics have been revised several times; the most recent change in 2018 made the anthem gender-neutral by changing 'all thy sons' to 'all of us'.

China.history: Originally the theme song for the 1935 film 'Children of Troubled Times', a story about volunteers fighting Japanese invaders in Northeast China.
China.funFact: During the Cultural Revolution, the lyricist Tian Han was imprisoned, and the anthem was played without lyrics or with alternative words for years.

France.history: Written in 1792 by Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle during the French Revolutionary Wars. It was a call to arms for the people to defend their country.
France.funFact: It was banned by Napoleon I, Louis XVIII, and Napoleon III for its revolutionary associations before being restored as the national anthem in 1879.

Germany.history: The melody was written by Joseph Haydn in 1797. The lyrics were written by Hoffmann von Fallersleben in 1841.
Germany.funFact: Since 1952, only the third stanza ('Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit') has been used as the national anthem to avoid associations with the first stanza's misuse by the Nazi regime.

Greece.history: The lyrics come from a massive poem of 158 stanzas written by Dionysios Solomos in 1823. It became the national anthem in 1865.
Greece.funFact: It is the longest national anthem in the world by text (158 stanzas), though only the first two are ever sung.

India.history: Written by Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore in 1911. It was officially adopted by the Constituent Assembly as the national anthem in 1950.
India.funFact: A formal rendition of the national anthem takes exactly 52 seconds. A shortened version consisting of the first and last lines takes about 20 seconds.

Italy.history: Also known as 'Fratelli d’Italia', it was written in 1847 by Goffredo Mameli. It was only officially made the de jure national anthem in 2017.
Italy.funFact: Goffredo Mameli was only 20 years old when he wrote the lyrics; he died just two years later in the struggle for Italian unification.

Japan.history: Its lyrics are among the world's oldest, based on a Waka poem from the Heian period. The music was composed in the late 19th century.
Japan.funFact: With only 32 characters, it has one of the shortest lyrics of any national anthem in the world.

Mexico.history: Adopted in 1854 after a national contest. The lyrics were written by Francisco González Bocanegra after his fiancée locked him in a room until he finished them.
Mexico.funFact: Mexico has very strict laws regarding the anthem; it is illegal to sing it incorrectly or use it for commercial purposes.

Netherlands.history: Dates back to at least 1572, making it the oldest national anthem in the world. It is written from the perspective of William of Orange.
Netherlands.funFact: The first letters of each of the 15 stanzas form the name 'Willem van Nassov', a common poetic device known as an acrostic.

Poland.history: Written in 1797 in Italy by Józef Wybicki for the Polish Legions serving under Napoleon. It expresses the hope that Poland will regain its independence.
Poland.funFact: The lyrics have inspired several other Slavic anthems, including the former anthem of Yugoslavia.

Portugal.history: Composed in response to the 1890 British Ultimatum. It was originally a revolutionary song for the republican movement before becoming the national anthem in 1911.
Portugal.funFact: One line was changed from 'Against the Britons, march, march!' to 'Against the cannons, march, march!' to avoid offending their oldest ally.

Russian Federation.anthem: State Anthem of the Russian Federation
Russian Federation.history: Adopted in 2000, it uses the music of the former Soviet Union anthem (composed by Alexander Alexandrov) with new lyrics by Sergey Mikhalkov.
Russian Federation.funFact: Sergey Mikhalkov also wrote the lyrics for the original 1944 Soviet anthem and its 1977 revision, making him the author of three different anthem versions.

South Africa.history: A unique hybrid anthem adopted in 1997. It combines the popular hymn 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika' with the former anthem 'Die Stem van Suid-Afrika'.
South Africa.funFact: It is the only national anthem in the world that moves through five different languages: isiXhosa, isiZulu, Sesotho, Afrikaans, and English.

South Korea.history: The name means 'The Patriotic Song'. The music was composed in 1935 by Ahn Eak-tai while he was in Spain, to replace a version sung to a Scottish folk tune.
South Korea.funFact: Before the current music was composed, the lyrics were often sung to the tune of 'Auld Lang Syne'.

Spain.history: One of the oldest anthems in the world, first appearing in 1761. It was originally a military march for the Spanish Infantry.
Spain.funFact: It is one of the few national anthems in the world that has no official lyrics, though several versions have been proposed over the years.

Switzerland.history: Composed in 1841 by Alberik Zwyssig, it was traditionally sung at national events for over a century before officially becoming the anthem in 1981.
Switzerland.funFact: The lyrics have official versions in all four national languages of Switzerland: German, French, Italian, and Romansh.

Turkey.history: Adopted in 1921 during the Turkish War of Independence. The lyrics by Mehmet Akif Ersoy were selected from 724 entries in a nationwide competition.
Turkey.funFact: Ersoy refused the prize money for winning the contest, as he felt he shouldn't be paid for writing a song for his nation.

Ukraine.anthem: Shche ne vmerla Ukrainy i slava, i volia
Ukraine.history: The lyrics were written in 1862 by Pavlo Chubynsky. It was briefly the anthem of the Ukrainian People's Republic in 1917 before being restored in 1992.
Ukraine.funFact: The title translates to 'The glory and the freedom of Ukraine has not yet perished', reflecting the nation's long struggle for independence.

United Kingdom.history: The origin of the words and music is obscure. It was first performed in a London theatre in 1745 and became known as the National Anthem in the early 19th century.
United Kingdom.funFact: The anthem has no single authorized version; it is a tradition rather than a law. The lyrics change from 'Queen' to 'King' depending on the current monarch.

United States.history: Lyrics were written in 1814 by Francis Scott Key after he saw the American flag still flying over Fort McHenry after a British bombardment.
United States.funFact: The music was actually taken from an old British drinking song called 'To Anacreon in Heaven'.
